source.title: Self-critiquing models for assisting human evaluators
source.authors: W. Saunders; Catherine Yeh; Jeff Wu; S. Bills; Long Ouyang; Jonathan Ward; Jan Leike

record.tranche_reason: Tests downstream critique and refinement scaling trends, using different tasks and measures from held-out pretraining loss scaling.
record.gate_note: The paper does not measure held-out pretraining cross-entropy, fit power laws to parameters, tokens, or compute, or test small-run extrapolation or compute-optimal allocations. It defines model scale using supervised fine-tuning validation loss and reports scaling results for critique and refinement tasks. Numerical values in the relevant plots are not stated in the text.
record.test_reason: In a new setting (fine-tuned critique and refinement tasks), the study reports how downstream task performance changes across five models ordered by fine-tuning validation loss. This bears on V6, but only on the direction of the trend. No law is fitted or extrapolated, and scale is fine-tuning loss, not pretraining loss or parameters. T3 fits better than the reader's T2, since the study does not aim at the scaling question itself.
record.authors_conclusion: Mostly correct. Add that model critiques help humans find about 50% more flaws. Add that larger models write more helpful critiques and refine better, with small models showing no refinement gain. Authors caution that positive critique scaling may not be fundamental and that the critique-discrimination gap shows no sign of closing.
record.recipe_differences: Studies supervised fine-tuning task performance across models, using fine-tuning validation loss as its scale measure; it does not reproduce pretraining-loss sweeps or fit the original power laws.
record.method_sensitivity: Performance varies with task: synthetic-task critique scaling is less clear than topic-based summarization. Refinement gains appear at larger scales but have little to no effect at smaller scales.

fits_no_version.finding: Generator-discriminator-critique gaps vs scale. GD and GC gaps are positive and may slightly increase. The CD gap is roughly constant for summarization and task-dependent for synthetic tasks. GC gains from best-of-N do not improve with model size (Figs 8, 9, 12, 13).
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Gaps between a model's discrimination and critique abilities do not close with scale.

record.problems: The paper says models are not directly comparable because their pretraining datasets differ. The authors note that the supervised training data contains more critiques of larger-model outputs, although they believe the effect is minimal. Topic-based summarization lacks robust objective ground truth, and the authors describe some results as noisy. Relevant plot values are not stated in the text.
record.rows_left_out: No additional claim-relevant result rows omitted.

untested.parts: No pretraining loss measured or fitted against parameters, tokens or compute.
No fits on small runs used to predict larger runs.
No shape or architecture comparison at fixed parameter count.
No power-law fit in another modality or regime; fine-tuned tasks are not fitted to any law.
Untested parts: a quantitative predictive relation, prediction from pretraining loss, extrapolation to larger models, and breadth across many downstream tasks.

missing.what: Base-task output quality vs scale. More capable models have critiqueable outputs about 20% less often than the smallest models, per labelers (Fig 4a/4c). This is a downstream scaling result bearing on V6.

record.verdict_notes: Scale is defined by SFT validation loss across five pretrained models that are not directly comparable (different pretraining data). No parameter counts are given. All scaling evidence is figure-only, with no numbers in the text. The study is weak evidence for V6: it shows direction of improvement, not predictability. The tranche was changed from T2 to T3.

versions.untested_parts: Held-out pretraining loss scaling with parameters, tokens, or compute.
Prediction of much larger runs from power laws fitted on smaller runs.
Architecture comparisons at fixed parameter count.
Power-law behavior in other modalities or training regimes.

The paper tests critique and refinement performance against its supervised fine-tuning validation-loss scale, not pretraining loss; it does not give a quantitative predictive law or test extrapolation to much larger models or a broad range of downstream tasks.
Dependence of loss-law exponents or compute-optimal allocations on fitting choices or setup.

rows.subject: five pre-trained models; individual model names not stated
rows.operation_detail: Compared self-critique helpfulness across model scales.

conditions.value: not filtered for answers humans found critiqueable

rows.uncertainty: z = 1 (one standard deviation), as stated for figure error bars
rows.note: The text says larger models are better at self-critiquing, including without filtering for critiqueable answers. Scale is defined using supervised fine-tuning validation loss.
rows.check: Scale axis is supervised fine-tuning validation loss, not parameters or pretraining loss. Values are figure-only. The text says larger models are significantly better at self-critiquing. 'Observed' covers improvement with scale, not predictability.

rows.subject: five pre-trained models; individual model names not stated
rows.operation_detail: Compared self-critique helpfulness across model scales.
rows.uncertainty: z = 1 (one standard deviation), as stated for figure error bars
rows.note: The text reports that larger models are better at self-critiquing even though their answers are harder to critique.
rows.check: Same caveats as r1. This is the 'critiqueable answers' curve in Fig 4b.

rows.subject: synthetic-task models (four tasks; individual model names not stated)
rows.operation_detail: Compared self-critique helpfulness across model scales.
rows.measure: Critique validity according to an oracle
rows.uncertainty: z = 1 (one standard deviation), as stated for figure error bars
rows.note: The authors report generally similar trends for critiqueable synthetic-task answers, but say the overall pattern is less clear. The plotted result covers the synthetic tasks; the text does not give separate task values.
rows.check: Authors say 'similar trends' but 'the story is less clear'. Synthetic-task models are each fine-tuned on qualitatively different second-round data, so scale is confounded with data.

rows.subject: five pre-trained models; individual model names not stated
rows.operation_detail: Compared critique-conditional refinement performance across model scales.
rows.measure: Win rate of refinement relative to the original best-of-1 answer
rows.baseline: original best-of-1 answer from the same model
rows.uncertainty: z = 1 (one standard deviation), as stated for figure error bars
rows.note: The text says critique-conditional refinements significantly outperform the original for larger models but have little to no effect for smaller models; results are described as somewhat noisy.
rows.check: Gains appear only for larger models, with 'little to no effect for smaller models'. Results are noisy. This is a threshold-like pattern, not a smooth predictable trend.

rows.subject: five pre-trained models; individual model names not stated
rows.operation_detail: Compared direct refinement performance across model scales.
rows.measure: Win rate of refinement relative to the original best-of-1 answer
rows.baseline: original best-of-1 answer from the same model
rows.uncertainty: z = 1 (one standard deviation), as stated for figure error bars
rows.note: The text says direct refinements significantly outperform the original for larger models but have little to no effect for smaller models. It also says best-of-8 direct refinement appears to be a stronger baseline than critique refinement.
rows.check: Same pattern as r4. Labelled 'comparator', but it is itself a scaling result for direct refinement.

relationships.condition: Topic-based summarization self-critique helpfulness, human-judged, five models ordered by SFT validation loss
relationships.reason: Larger models write more helpful self-critiques with or without filtering for critiqueable answers (r1, r2). This shows direction only, figure-only, with no fitted law.
relationships.display_finding: Larger models produced more helpful self-critiques both with and without filtering for critiqueable answers, although no scaling law was fitted.

relationships.reason: The synthetic-task trend is less consistent (r3). Refinement gains are absent at small scale and appear only for larger models, and are noisy (r4, r5). Authors see no strong reason the trend is fundamental.
relationships.display_finding: Synthetic-task trends were inconsistent, and summarization refinement gains appeared only at larger scales with substantial noise.

source_check.scope: Only the listed rows, labels and statements were checked; presence is not whole-study approval.
